title: Machines: EC2, AMIs and launch templates
bridge: An EC2 instance is like a CI runner you rent by the second. An AMI is like the Docker image it boots from. Except the image is a whole disk with no layers, and the machine can ask a local address for its role's credentials. That address is the first thing an attacker on the VM tries.
intro: Every run gets a fresh VM. This lesson picks its size, boots it from our image, and writes the launch template that sets its rules. Those rules are: no public IP, an encrypted disk, a near-empty role, and a metadata service the agent cannot reach.

picture.caption: The launch template turns last night's image into a VM with fixed rules; the metadata door stays shut to the agent.

steps.text: resolve:ssm: reads the promoted image ID at launch time
points at the image that passed last night's smoke test
boots with the template's type, disk, role and security group
root's SSM agent asks for the role's credentials, with a token
the agent, or a container, tries the same address
refused: wrong user, no token, or one network hop too far

p: An instance type names a machine shape. m8i.2xlarge reads as: family m (general purpose), generation 8, i for Intel, size 2xlarge. Each size up doubles the CPUs and memory.

We use one image and three sizes (G3-11). lite is m8i.xlarge for plans and small routines. full is m8i.2xlarge for builds with FCP Lab. wide is m8i.4xlarge for the heaviest work. A full VM costs about $0.42 an hour while it runs (G3-20); a stopped one costs only its disk.
sections.because: We read the sizes from the API rather than a blog because the numbers decide what FCP Lab can run.

code.text:
aws ec2 describe-instance-types \
  --instance-types m8i.xlarge m8i.2xlarge m8i.4xlarge \
  --query 'InstanceTypes[].[InstanceType,VCpuInfo.DefaultVCpus,MemoryInfo.SizeInMiB]' \
  --output text

notes.text: The three sandbox sizes: lite, full and wide.
vCPUs and memory in MiB. 16384 MiB is 16 GiB.
Text output is quick to scan in a terminal. moto knows the real shapes.

sections.h: AMIs: the disk a VM starts from
p: An AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is a saved disk plus a few settings. A VM boots from it. An AMI belongs to one account and one region; other accounts can use it only if it is shared with them.

Our images are built by Packer in the inf account (p4-4) and shared with ai-agents (infrastructure PR #1724). They are named rhino-ai-agent-sandbox-v<N>-<testing|release>-<time>. A launch template does not name an AMI ID. It names an SSM parameter, so promoting a new image is one parameter write (G3-16).
sections.because: We store the image ID in a parameter because then three launch templates never need editing when the image changes.

code.text:
aws ssm put-parameter --name /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id \
  --type String --data-type aws:ec2:image --value ami-03cf127a
aws ssm get-parameter --name /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id \
  --query Parameter.Value --output text
# a launch template then says: ImageId = resolve:ssm:/ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id

notes.text: data-type aws:ec2:image makes AWS check that the value is a real AMI ID.
Anyone may read it back; the value is not a secret.
resolve:ssm: means 'read this parameter when you launch'. A new value applies to the next VM.

sections.h: A launch template: every setting in one place
p: A launch template is a saved set of answers for 'start a VM'. Image, type, role, network, disk, metadata rules, tags. Auto Scaling groups (p3-4) and the smoke test both start VMs from it, so every VM gets the same rules.
Below is the lite template as JSON for the CLI. G3-11 writes the same in Terraform (p4-3), one per size.
sections.because: We put the rules in the template because a rule that every caller must remember gets forgotten.

notes.text: The promoted image, read at launch.
The instance profile from p3-1: SSM core and one lifecycle action, nothing else.
IMDSv2 only: every metadata request needs a token (next section).
Hop limit 1: the token cannot travel past the VM's own network stack.
gp3 is the general SSD type. 120 GiB, encrypted. G3-11 also names the sandbox KMS key here.
The sweeper (p3-7) finds VMs and disks only by these tags. G3-11 tags the volume too.

callout.text: There is no network setting with a public IP. The Auto Scaling group places VMs in the private subnets, and the template names the sandbox security group.

sections.h: The metadata service: what a VM knows
p: Every VM can reach 169.254.169.254, the instance metadata service (IMDS). It answers questions about the VM itself: its ID, its role, a Spot warning, its Auto Scaling state.
It also hands out the role's temporary credentials. Any program on the VM that can open a connection there gets them. That is the door an attacker tries first.
IMDSv2 adds a step: first PUT a request for a short token, then send the token with every GET. A plain GET, the IMDSv1 way, gets 401 Unauthorized when tokens are required.
sections.because: We show the token dance because spot-watch (p3-4) and the warm-up script both use it.

code.file: on a real sandbox VM, as root
code.text:
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token \
  -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 300")
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id

notes.text: Step 1 of IMDSv2: a PUT that returns a token. Tricks that make a server fetch a URL for an attacker usually cannot send this PUT.
Step 2: every read carries the token.
Lists the role name. Adding the name to the path returns the credentials.
No token: refused with 401 because the template says HttpTokens required.

sections.see:
i-0abc1234def567890
ai-agent-sandbox
401
(on a real VM; your IDs differ)

sections.h: Hop limit 1 and the host rules
p: Each network hop lowers a packet's hop count. With a hop limit of 1, the token reply dies after one hop. A container on the Docker bridge is one hop further away, so it never gets a token.

The agent's own user is not in a container, so G3-08 adds host rules in the image. An iptables rule lets only root (user ID 0) reach 169.254.169.254. Root runs the SSM agent, which needs it. A rule in the DOCKER-USER chain, Docker's place for your own rules, drops it for containers.
sections.because: We check before we add each rule, because the image role runs on every build and must not stack copies.

code.text:
iptables -C OUTPUT -d 169.254.169.254 -m owner ! --uid-owner 0 -j REJECT 2>/dev/null ||
  iptables -A OUTPUT -d 169.254.169.254 -m owner ! --uid-owner 0 -j REJECT
iptables -C DOCKER-USER -d 169.254.169.254 -j DROP 2>/dev/null ||
  iptables -I DOCKER-USER -d 169.254.169.254 -j DROP
netfilter-persistent save

notes.text: -C checks whether the rule exists. The || runs line 2 only if it does not.
-m owner matches the user that sent the packet. Everyone except uid 0 is rejected.
-I inserts at the top of DOCKER-USER, so it runs before Docker's own rules.
Saves the rules so they survive a reboot. Warm VMs are stopped and started (p3-4).

callout.text: These rules are speed bumps: root can delete them, and the docker group gives root. The wall is p3-1's near-empty role. A stolen credential can complete a lifecycle hook and talk to SSM, nothing more.

p: The root disk is an EBS volume: network storage that outlives a stop. G3-11 makes it gp3, 120 GiB, encrypted with the sandbox key from KMS, AWS's key service. The key policy must allow the AutoScaling service-linked role, the role AWS's Auto Scaling uses to act for you. Otherwise the group cannot launch VMs with that key.

A volume made from an AMI is slow on its first read of each block. G3-11 sets volume_initialization_rate to 300 MiB/s to fill it faster; check that the pinned aws provider 6.64.0 supports it. Tags ai-agents:managed and ai-agents:size go on the VM and the volume, so the sweeper can find orphans.

callout.text: If the KMS key policy misses the AutoScaling service-linked role, launches fail with a key error. The warm pool then stays empty.

lab.alone: Write a second template, ai-agents-sandbox-wide, for m8i.4xlarge with the same metadata options and the tag ai-agents:size = wide. Create it in moto. Then write one describe-launch-template-versions call per template that prints the instance type and HttpTokens, and check both say required.

quiz.q: Why does the launch template set a hop limit of 1?

options.text: So the token reply dies at the Docker bridge and containers cannot get a token
options.why: The reply needs a second hop to reach a container; with a limit of 1 it is dropped.

options.text: So the VM has only one network card
options.why: Hop limit is about how far a packet travels, not how many cards a VM has.

options.text: So IMDS answers one request per second
options.why: It is not a rate limit.

quiz.q: A new image passed the smoke test. What makes the next VMs use it?

options.text: Editing the three launch templates and applying Terraform
options.why: That is the work resolve:ssm saves us.

options.text: Restarting every warm VM by hand
options.why: Warm VMs are replaced over time by the sweeper (p3-7); no hand restarts.

options.text: Writing its ID into /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id; templates read it at launch
options.why: One parameter write promotes it, and the previous ID is kept for rollback (p4-4).

quiz.q: The docker group makes the agent root-equivalent. What is the real wall around the role's credentials?

options.text: The instance role holds almost nothing worth stealing
options.why: Assume the credentials leak. They can only finish a lifecycle hook and talk to SSM.
Root on the VM can request a token like the SSM agent does.

words.plain: A machine shape such as m8i.2xlarge: family, generation, processor and size.
Amazon Machine Image: a saved disk a VM boots from, owned by one account in one region.
A saved set of settings for starting a VM: image, type, role, disk, metadata rules, tags.
The instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which tells a VM about itself and hands out its role's credentials.
The metadata mode where every read needs a token from a PUT first.
How many network hops the token reply may travel; 1 keeps it away from containers.
A network disk attached to a VM that survives a stop; ours is gp3, 120 GiB, encrypted.

tickets.why: One launch template per size with IMDSv2, hop limit 1, an encrypted gp3 disk, no public IP and the near-empty role.
The image's host rules: only root reaches the metadata address, containers never, saved across reboots.

remember: The launch template fixes every VM's rules. The metadata door is shut to the agent, and the role behind it holds nothing worth stealing.
